one-feature edit of PBG-LFNDPIECEKING1-8: black pawn added on g6 guarding the bishop

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king on d4 can step to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can step to.

hints: The king moves one square. Which squares touch it?
Count the squares around the king, straight and diagonal. Is any of them attacked here?
Nothing black is near, so every neighbouring square counts: eight in all.
items.explain: The king steps one square in any direction, straight or diagonal. In the middle of an empty board it has all eight neighbouring squares, and the far-away black king attacks none of them.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king on e1 can step to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can step to.

hints: The king moves one square. Which neighbouring squares are on the board?
The king stands on the edge, so the row below it does not exist.
Five squares: the two beside it and the three in front.
items.explain: On the edge of the board some neighbours do not exist, so the king on e1 has five squares. The black king is far away and attacks none of them.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king on e3 can step to. Watch the black knight.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can step to.
The knight on g5 attacks e4.
The knight on g5 attacks f3.

hints: List the eight neighbours first, then ask which of them the knight attacks.
A knight attacks the squares at the end of its L-shaped jump. From g5 that includes two squares next to the king.
The knight on g5 attacks e4 and f3, so the king has six squares left.
items.explain: The knight on g5 jumps to e4 and f3, both next to the king, so those two are forbidden. The other six neighbours are free.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king on f5 can step to. Watch the black pawn.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can step to.
Nothing black attacks f6.
The pawn on f7 attacks e6.
The pawn on f7 attacks g6.

hints: Black pawns move down the board. Which two squares does the pawn on f7 attack?
A pawn attacks the squares diagonally in front of it, not the square straight ahead.
The pawn attacks e6 and g6. The square f6 in front of it is not attacked.
items.explain: The black pawn on f7 attacks e6 and g6, one step diagonally forward. It does not attack f6, the square directly in front of it, so the king may step there.

items.prompt: Can the white king capture the black knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The king can capture on d5.
No black piece attacks d5.

hints: Is the knight on a neighbouring square? Yes. So ask which black piece attacks d5.
The bishop on a8 would see d5 along a diagonal. Is anything standing in its way?
The pawn on b7 blocks the bishop's diagonal, and the pawn itself attacks only a6 and c6.
items.explain: The bishop on a8 would guard d5, but the pawn on b7 stands in its path, so the bishop sees nothing beyond b7. No black piece attacks d5, and the king may take the knight.

items.prompt: White to move. The king can capture exactly one of the two black knights. Find the move.

claims.statement: The king can capture the knight on d3.
The king cannot capture the knight on d5.
No black piece guards d3.
The pawn on c6 guards d5.

hints: Both knights stand next to the king. For each one, ask whether a black piece guards its square.
Look at the knight on d5 first: which black piece attacks that square?
The pawn on c6 guards d5, so the king must take the other knight.
items.explain: The pawn on c6 guards the knight on d5, so the king may not take it. Nothing guards the knight on d3, so the king takes that one for free.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king can step to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king can step to.
The rook on a3 attacks e3.
The bishop on b8 attacks e5.

hints: Check each of the eight neighbours against both black pieces.
One black piece attacks along a rank, the other along a diagonal.
Three squares are free. The rook covers the third rank and the bishop covers a long diagonal.
items.explain: The rook on a3 attacks d3, e3 and f3 along the third rank. The bishop on b8 attacks e5 and f4 along its diagonal. That leaves d4, d5 and f5.

items.prompt: Can the white king capture the black bishop on f5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The king can capture on f5.
No black piece guards f5.

hints: The bishop stands on a neighbouring square. Which black piece could take back on f5?
items.explain: No black piece attacks f5, so the king may take the bishop.

items.prompt: A black pawn now stands on g6. Can the white king capture the black bishop on f5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The king cannot capture on f5.
The pawn on g6 guards f5.

hints: Look at what changed. Which black piece attacks f5 now?
Black pawns capture diagonally downward. The pawn on g6 attacks f5 and h5.
items.explain: The pawn on g6 guards f5. If the king took the bishop it would land on an attacked square, which is never allowed.
